item.title: The Architecture of Midnight: Solitude, Waxing Candles, and the Prairie Void
item.description:
There is a moment, typically around half-past eleven on a Manitoba autumn night, when the house settles into its foundations and the world outside ceases its ceaseless mechanical hum. The wind off the stubble fields drops to a low murmur against the double-paned glass. The blue light of monitors is banished; only the warm, trembling amber of a beeswax candle remains.

In this sanctuary of shadow, thought finally slows down enough to be examined.

item.title: Marginalia in the Dark: Conversations with Dead Philosophers and Worn Leather Covers
item.description:
In the corner of my study stands an oak bookcase filled with volumes that smell of dry paper, animal glue, and aged leather. Many of these books were bought for fifty cents at rural estate sales across the Westman area—salvaged from old parlor boxes and estate auctions in Minnedosa, Souris, and Neepawa.

When you open a volume of Marcus Aurelius printed in 1904 or an antique collection of Edgar Allan Poe’s tales bound in dark cloth, you are never alone.
